name: Strip-based, seepage and filtering models for two-wheelers in mixed traffic
type: model (family: strip/sublane lateral discretisation, queue-model seepage, 2D force-based filtering) plus one benchmark dataset
maintainer: Strip-based: Mathew, Munigety and Bajpai, IIT Bombay (SiMTraM on SUMO); Gunay (2007) lateral-discomfort staggered following. Seepage in MATSim: Amit Agarwal and Gregor Laemmel (TU Berlin VSP / Forschungszentrum Juelich), 2015-2016. 2D filtering: Kanagaraj and Treiber (IIT Madras / TU Dresden) 2018; Ni, Li, Yuan, Sun (Tongji University / TU Delft) 2023 multi-interaction framework. Benchmark: Guin, Bazan-Guillen, Kannan, Lu, Postigo-Boix (Universitat Politecnica de Catalunya), Mendeley Data 2026. SUMO sublane model: Eclipse SUMO / DLR.
first_release: 2007 (Gunay lateral discomfort); 2015 (Agarwal and Laemmel, Procedia Computer Science 52, 890-895); 2015 (Mathew et al. strip-based, J. Comput. Civ. Eng.; some references list 2013) ; 2016 (Agarwal and Laemmel journal version, Transportation in Developing Economies 2); 2023 (Ni et al., Physica A 611, 128441).
last_activity: 11 July 2026: Mendeley Data 'Dataset for Modeling and benchmarking two-wheeler seepage behavior in dense mixed traffic simulations' v1, DOI 10.17632/hs6drgb2vx.1.
licence: Papers: publisher copyright (Agarwal and Laemmel 2016 is Springer; working-paper PDF freely available from TU Berlin VSP). MATSim code: GPL-2.0 [uncertain on exact version]. SUMO: EPL-2.0. Mendeley benchmark dataset: CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial). Ni et al. 2023: paywalled, no code found.
language: MATSim seepage: Java (MATSim QSim). SiMTraM: C++ on SUMO [uncertain]. Kanagaraj-Treiber MTM: MATLAB for calibration; JavaScript demo in Treiber's mixedTraffic. Ni et al.: not stated.
code_availability: MATSim seepage: implemented inside MATSim's queue simulation (QSim 'seep modes' configuration) [uncertain on current config key names; check MATSim qsim config group]. SUMO sublane: open source (https://github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo). Strip-based SiMTraM: paper only, no public repo found. Ni et al. 2023 multi-interaction: paper only. Mendeley benchmark: data only (processed detections, seepage event annotations, simulation calibration outputs; raw IDD/TIAND video not included).
maintenance_health: SUMO sublane model is actively maintained. MATSim seepage was a research feature from 2015-2016; whether it is still maintained in current MATSim releases is unclear [uncertain]. Strip-based SiMTraM and the Tongji/TU Delft framework appear to be one-off research code. The UPC benchmark is new (July 2026) with no linked paper yet.
scale: Microscopic (strip-based, sublane, 2D force models) and mesoscopic queue-based (MATSim seepage: link-level FIFO queue with earliest-exit times).
car_following: Strip-based models use a car-following model per strip set (SiMTraM: modified Gipps-like / SUMO Krauss [uncertain]); MTM uses IDM/ACC (motorcycle T 0.3 s, s0 0.5 m, a 2 m/s2); MATSim seepage has no car-following, only link travel time = length / min(link max speed, vehicle max speed) plus flow/storage capacity.
lane_model: Strip-based: road divided into narrow longitudinal strips; a vehicle occupies ceil(width / strip width) adjacent strips; lane change = shift by one or more strips. SUMO sublane: lane divided into sublanes of --lateral-resolution width (e.g. 0.8 m on a 3.2 m lane); lateral position continuous, occupancy computed at sublane granularity. MATSim: no lanes, link is a queue.
lateral_model_type: Strip-based (Mathew et al.), sublane (SUMO SL2015), continuous 2D force-based (Kanagaraj-Treiber MTM; Ni et al. behaviour force model), none (MATSim seepage queue).
junction_model: MATSim seepage: at link exit, seep-mode vehicles in the queue jump to the front and leave subject to link flow capacity and downstream storage capacity; junction priority otherwise as standard MATSim. SiMTraM claims intersection coverage [uncertain on rules]. SUMO sublane: standard SUMO junction logic; two-wheelers can stop side-by-side in a lane at the stop line.
signal_control_modes: Not specific to these models; signal acts as a queue stopper. Seepage matters most at signals (two-wheelers collect at the stop line and discharge first).
flyover_support: Not applicable to the lateral/seepage logic (link-level behaviour).
vehicle_types: MATSim seepage: car (PCU 1, 16.67 m/s), motorbike (PCU 0.25, 16.67 m/s), bike/bicycle (PCU 0.25, 4.17 m/s); seep modes configurable (motorbike, bike). MTM: motorcycle, car, bus, auto-rickshaw. Ni et al.: bicycles, e-bicycles, e-mopeds. Mendeley benchmark: two-wheelers in Indian dense traffic (IDD/TIAND imagery).
gridlock_policy: MATSim backward-travelling holes create inflow capacity; seepage with unrestricted seep vehicles starved cars (car flow fluctuated, no steady state above 110 PCU/km), fixed by 'restricted seepage' (after 4 seeping bikes, the queue head must leave). Otherwise not specified.
mixed_traffic_support: Yes, this is the central purpose: lets small vehicles share road width and overtake/filter large ones.
non_lane_behaviour: IMPLEMENTABLE RULE SET (synthesised from Mathew et al. strip-based approach, SUMO sublane semantics and Kanagaraj-Treiber MTM; numbers cited). (1) Discretise each road segment laterally into strips of width w_s, at most the narrowest vehicle width (SUMO guidance; e.g. 0.5 m for 0.6-0.73 m two-wheelers, or 0.8 m on a 3.2 m lane). Mathew et al. found strip width = lane width reproduces lane-based throughput; small strips approximate continuous lateral motion. (2) A vehicle occupies k = ceil((W + minGapLat) / w_s) contiguous strips; two vehicles may not occupy the same strip while longitudinally overlapping. (3) Leader for car-following = nearest vehicle ahead occupying any of the follower's strips (lateral overlap). Compute IDM acceleration a_0 for current strip set. (4) Each step (or every 0.5-1 s), for candidate offsets of -n..+n strips (n limited by max lateral speed * dt; observed two-wheeler lateral speed P90 ~0.3 m/s, max ~1.6-2.2 m/s; cars SD ~0.09 m/s), compute the IDM acceleration a_j against the leader in the candidate strip set and the induced deceleration on the new follower. (5) Move to the candidate maximising a_j - a_0 - p*(induced braking on new follower) if gain > threshold (MOBIL-style; MTM politeness p = 0.2) and lateral clearance >= minGapLat to neighbours (MTM soft lateral gap ~0.15-0.30 m). (6) Gap filling at standstill: when speed < ~1 m/s and the gap ahead in current strips is < s0, a two-wheeler searches strips within its reach for a longitudinal gap >= its length + s0 and creeps forward at low speed (seepage). (7) Larger vehicles (car, bus) are restricted to lateral moves of whole-vehicle size and prefer lane-centre alignment; two-wheelers use 'arbitrary/compact' alignment. (8) Road edges act as boundaries with clearance (MTM boundary scale 0.15-0.25 m).
seepage_filtering_support: AGARWAL AND LAEMMEL 2016 MATSIM ALGORITHM (exact from paper): passing queue model first computes for each vehicle on a link t_earliest = link_length / min(v_link_max, v_vehicle_max); vehicles are sorted by t_earliest so faster vehicles overtake in free flow. A vehicle is 'queued' when current time t > t_earliest. Seepage queue model: at every time step for every link, if any vehicle is queued, scan queued vehicles; the first one whose mode is a seep mode is moved to the front of the queue (then break for that link); the front vehicle then leaves if link flow capacity and next-link storage capacity allow; if no seep vehicle is found, normal FIFO exit. Seepage is not allowed between two vehicles of the same type. Multiple seep modes allowed (motorbike and bike). RESTRICTED SEEPAGE (Algorithm 2): counter m per link; while m <= 4, a seep vehicle is pushed to the front and m++; else m = 0 and the regular queue head leaves - i.e. after every 4 seeping bikes (4 x 0.25 PCU = 1 PCU) the head vehicle gets to go; authors note this 4 must be calibrated. BACKWARD-TRAVELLING HOLES: each vehicle leaving the downstream end creates a hole of size = its PCU that travels upstream at a constant 15 km/h (about 1.8 s headway); upstream entry is allowed only when holes have arrived, giving an inflow capacity and a triangular fundamental diagram. Parameters used: car PCU 1, 16.67 m/s; motorbike PCU 0.25, 16.67 m/s; bike PCU 0.25, 4.17 m/s; test track 3 x 1000 m links, capacity 2700 PCU/h, jam density 133.33 PCU/km. SUMO equivalent: sublane model lets motorcycles pass within a lane; pair with lcPushy/lcAssertive/lcImpatience to squeeze through. MTM equivalent: lateral force toward space where acceleration is higher produces filtering naturally. MULTI-INTERACTION (Ni, Li, Yuan, Sun 2023, Physica A 611:128441): three layers per two-wheeler per step - (a) perception: Comfort Zone model selects the set of road users interacting simultaneously; (b) decision: Bayesian network chooses the manoeuvre (e.g. follow, overtake left/right, yield) given multi-interaction states; (c) execution: behaviour force model (social-force-like attraction to target and repulsion from neighbours/boundaries) produces non-lane movement. Calibrated on Chinese bicycle/e-bike/e-moped trajectories; parameters not available in open text [uncertain].
per_class_parameters: MATSim seepage: car PCU 1 / 16.67 m/s; motorbike PCU 0.25 / 16.67 m/s; bike PCU 0.25 / 4.17 m/s; hole speed 15 km/h. MTM (Chennai): motorcycle 1.8 x 0.6 m, T 0.3 s, s0 0.5 m, a 2 m/s2; car 4.2 x 1.7 m; bus 10.3 x 2.1 m; auto 2.6 x 0.9 m [uncertain width as printed]; lateral parameters theta_max 0.2 rad, s_y0 0.15 m (braking), 0.30 m (steering), boundary 0.15 / 0.25 m, lambda 0.4 s, tau 1 s, lambda_dw 0.7 s/m, p 0.2. Observed lateral kinematics, Chennai 2023 congested (Agrawal et al. 2026): lateral speed SD TW 0.25 m/s, AR 0.15, car 0.09, HCV 0.10; lateral accel SD TW 0.18 m/s2, car 0.08; widths median TW 0.73 m, AR 1.35 m, car 1.85 m. SUMO sublane defaults: lcSublane 1.0, lcPushy 0, lcAssertive 0, lcImpatience 0.
indian_calibration_evidence: Mathew et al. strip-based model calibrated and validated on Mumbai data, strip parameter lambda calibrated against number of strip changes (values not retrieved) [uncertain]. Kanagaraj-Treiber MTM: Chennai, within 20% on travel time and flows; lateral shifts 11 observed vs 14 simulated (medium), 14 vs 9 (congested). Agarwal-Laemmel: Patna evacuation case (3505 nodes, 7542 links, 1% sample, bike as seep mode): Nash-equilibrium average trip time bike 178.47 -> 147.00 min (-17.6%), car 123.42 -> 170.91 min (+38.5%), motorbike 152.46 -> 214.33 min (+40.5%); total clearance time unchanged. This is a demonstration, not a calibration against observed data. Mendeley UPC benchmark (2026): seepage event annotations from Indian Driving Dataset (IDD) and TIAND videos plus simulation calibration outputs - the only open seepage-specific data found.
calibration_dataset_used: Mumbai (Mathew et al.; not open), Chennai arterial video (Kanagaraj et al. 2015), Patna Comprehensive Mobility Plan 2009 for demand (Agarwal-Laemmel; synthetic demonstration), Chinese trajectory data (Ni et al.), IDD and TIAND videos (UPC benchmark; raw data from idd.insaan.iiit.ac.in, processed data CC BY-NC 4.0 on Mendeley).
calibration_method: Mathew et al.: calibrate strip parameter against observed strip-change counts. MTM: genetic algorithm on 5 macroscopic measures. Agarwal-Laemmel: no calibration; validation via fundamental diagrams and sensitivity to bike share; the restricted-seepage count (4) explicitly flagged as needing scenario survey data. UPC benchmark: simulation calibration outputs included (method not described on landing page) [uncertain].
max_density_tested: MATSim seepage FD: up to ~110 PCU/km for bikes before data points vanish (unrestricted), jam density 133.33 PCU/km. MTM congested: 450 motorcycles/km + 225 cars/km + 35 buses/km + 80 autos/km on ~12 m roadway.
validation_against_field_case: Patna evacuation (illustrative), Chennai six-lane arterial (MTM), Mumbai (strip-based). No Bengaluru case found.
reuse_mode: Port the model. For a 72-hour web build implement a strip-based lateral model (rules above) on top of IDM; add the Agarwal-Laemmel queue-jump rule as a cheap 'seepage at stop line' behaviour (with a restricted-seepage counter) if a full lateral model is cut. Use the Mendeley UPC benchmark as validation data for seepage rates (non-commercial licence). Treat Ni et al. 2023 as inspiration only (paywalled, Chinese two-wheelers, too complex).
effort_within_72_hours: Option A, queue-jump seepage on a lane/link queue (Agarwal-Laemmel): 2-3 hours; very robust, gives the visible effect of two-wheelers at the front of the queue at signals. Option B, strip-based lateral model (strips 0.5 m, leader by strip overlap, MOBIL-style strip shift, standstill gap filling): 10-16 hours including debugging of overlap/collision checks and rendering; this is the realistic upper bound inside 72 hours. Option C, continuous 2D force model (MTM or Ni et al.): 20+ hours plus tuning instability risk - cut. Recommended: B with A's restricted-seepage counter as a safety valve at stop lines; cut Bayesian decision layers, comfort zones and calibration.
licence_constraint: Reimplementing algorithms from papers imposes nothing. Copying MATSim code would impose GPL [uncertain version]; copying SUMO code imposes EPL-2.0. The Mendeley benchmark is CC BY-NC 4.0: attribution required and no commercial use - fine for a non-commercial demo, a blocker if the simulator is sold.
known_limitations: Agarwal-Laemmel: seep vehicles do not save storage space (they still consume link storage even though they fit between cars); unrestricted seepage starves large vehicles and produced no congested-branch data above ~110 PCU/km; restriction factor 4 is arbitrary; consistency with kinematic wave theory under seepage is unclear; queue model has no geometry so it cannot show where two-wheelers are laterally. Strip-based: results depend on strip width; coarse strips give lane-like behaviour, fine strips raise computation; lateral moves are discrete jumps. SUMO sublane: smaller resolution increases computation; lateral extents computed only at resolution granularity; lane changes take multiple steps. MTM: lateral shift count mismatched in congestion. Ni et al.: validated only by face validation on non-Indian two-wheelers (bicycles, e-bikes, e-mopeds).
documented_failures: Agarwal and Laemmel 2015 (Procedia CS) fundamental diagrams lacked a proper congested branch; fixed in 2016 by adding backward-travelling holes and restricted seepage. In the Patna run, seepage made bikes 17.6% faster but cars and motorbikes 38-41% slower, showing seepage redistributes rather than adds capacity in a queue model.
validation_approach: Fundamental diagrams on a 3 x 1000 m triangular race track with varying mode shares (MATSim); sensitivity analysis on bike share; travel-time and flow comparisons against video (MTM); strip-change counts (strip-based); face validation against trajectories (Ni et al.); seepage-event annotations (UPC benchmark).
takeaway_for_our_build: Model lateral space explicitly with strips of 0.5 m (no wider than a two-wheeler), letting each vehicle occupy ceil((width + lateral clearance)/0.5) strips, and pick the car-following leader by strip overlap. Allow two-wheelers (and optionally autos) to shift strips when it increases their IDM acceleration and leaves >= 0.2-0.3 m lateral clearance, capped at a lateral speed of ~1 m/s. At stop lines implement explicit seepage: when stopped, two-wheelers may advance into any strip gap ahead long enough for them, and as a fallback apply the Agarwal-Laemmel rule (seep modes jump to the queue front, with a counter forcing the queue head to discharge after N seeps, default N = 4 and user-editable). Expose 'seepage on/off' and N as scenario controls and report per-class delay so users can see the redistribution effect (two-wheelers gain, cars lose) documented in the Patna case.
